userInput.lessonDescription: Turn duplicated code into a reusable function by naming the repeated job, making the changing parts parameters, and returning the useful result. Practice choosing what should stay inside the function and what should be supplied by each call.

steps.text: Suppose two places contain `const totalA = 20 * 1.08` and `const totalB = 35 * 1.08`. The values differ, but both blocks perform the same job: adding tax to a subtotal.
steps.title: Spot the repeated job

steps.text: Name the job by what it produces, such as `totalWithTax`. A clear name gives the repeated steps one purpose instead of describing how they happen.
steps.title: Name the result, not the steps

steps.text: Separate what changes from what stays the same. The subtotal and tax rate can change for each sale; multiplying the subtotal by `1 + taxRate` is the shared rule.
steps.title: Find the changing parts

steps.text: Turn the changing parts into parameters: `function totalWithTax(subtotal, taxRate) { return subtotal * (1 + taxRate); }`. Parameters are input slots that each call fills.
steps.title: Build the reusable function

steps.text: `return` sends the calculated value back to the caller. That lets other code store it, display it, compare it, or use it in another calculation instead of trapping it inside the function.
steps.title: Return the useful result

steps.text: Replace each copied calculation with a call: `const totalA = totalWithTax(20, 0.08)` and `const totalB = totalWithTax(35, 0.08)`. The supplied values are the arguments for that call.
steps.title: Replace copies with calls

steps.text: Keep the shared calculation inside the function. Keep page updates or `console.log` outside unless displaying is truly part of the named job; callers may want to use the returned total in different ways.
steps.title: Choose a clean boundary

steps.text: Add a parameter only when it represents a real input to the same job. If flags make one function calculate tax, print receipts, and update the page, split those into separate functions instead.
steps.title: Avoid overgeneralizing

steps.text: After extraction, run the old examples and compare their results. A good refactor removes duplication without changing behavior, while giving future fixes one clear place to make.
steps.title: Confirm the behavior

steps.conclusion: The training pipeline prompt calls its sequence an “exact order,” although the source explicitly says scheduler timing varies by framework; it should present this as a typical order. The final monitoring prompt shows warning traces but does not clearly visualize the diagnostic relationships—constant clipping versus threshold or training health, early spikes versus warmup or peak rate, and poor validation versus excessive weight decay. Also, appending each step title after an em dash may cause unnecessary subtitle text to be rendered.

Revise the pipeline label to “typical order” and optionally include a very short “check framework docs” note. Make the monitoring view more instructional by focusing on a few direct signal-to-response annotations, such as “early spike → more warmup/lower peak LR” and “constant clipping → inspect threshold or instability,” rather than merely displaying multiple traces and alerts.

userInput.lessonDescription: Use AdamW, learning-rate warmup and decay, and gradient clipping as core safeguards for stable Transformer training. Compare what each tool controls and why none of them replaces the others.

steps.text: Transformers contain many interacting attention and residual layers. An update that is merely large in one part of the model can spread, spike the loss, overflow mixed-precision numbers, or produce `NaN` values.
steps.title: Why training can become unstable

steps.text: AdamW tracks a moving average of each parameter’s gradient, \(m\), and squared gradient, \(v\). It updates roughly as \(\Delta\theta=-\eta\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat v}+\epsilon)\), giving each parameter an adaptive step size.
steps.title: AdamW adapts each update

steps.text: AdamW applies **weight decay** separately: \(\theta\leftarrow(1-\eta\lambda)\theta+\Delta\theta\). Here \(\eta\) is the learning rate and \(\lambda\) is decay strength; this separation avoids mixing shrinkage into Adam’s gradient scaling.
steps.title: Weight decay is separate

steps.text: Learning-rate **warmup** raises \(\eta\) gradually from near zero to its target during the first training steps. This prevents large early moves while gradients, optimizer averages, and internal activation patterns are still changing quickly.
steps.title: Warmup protects the start

steps.text: After warmup, the learning rate usually falls with a linear or cosine schedule. Large earlier steps learn broad patterns; smaller later steps reduce bouncing and let training settle near a useful solution.
steps.title: Decay settles the training

steps.text: Learning-rate decay and weight decay are different. Learning-rate decay shrinks every optimization step over time; weight decay continuously nudges parameter values toward zero as a form of regularization.
steps.title: Two meanings of decay

steps.text: Gradient clipping measures the combined gradient norm \(\lVert g\rVert\). If it exceeds threshold \(C\), use \(g\leftarrow g\min(1,C/(\lVert g\rVert+\epsilon))\), shrinking a spike while preserving its overall direction.
steps.title: Clipping catches gradient spikes

steps.text: A typical step is: compute gradients, unscale them if using mixed precision, clip their norm, run the AdamW update, then advance the learning-rate schedule. Frameworks differ on scheduler timing, so follow their documented order.
steps.title: Put the safeguards in order

steps.text: AdamW controls how gradients become parameter updates. Warmup and decay control the update scale over training time, while clipping limits exceptional gradient magnitude; none performs the other two jobs.
steps.title: Each tool controls something different

steps.text: Track loss, gradient norm, learning rate, and `NaN` or overflow events. Constant clipping suggests the threshold is too low or training is unhealthy; early spikes suggest more warmup or a lower peak rate, while poor validation may signal excessive weight decay.
steps.title: Read the warning signs

steps.conclusion: Prompt 5 risks collapsing a raid, ritual gathering, symbolic meanings, and immediate casualties into one generic action scene. This can misleadingly imply that ritual and combat occurred simultaneously, while the repeated symbol cannot clearly communicate courage, grief, identity, and remembered enemies. Prompt 0 also assigns one conflict pattern to each community, which may unintentionally suggest fixed regional types rather than several possible, varying practices. Prompt 8's visual idea of translation, disease, slavery, and disruption literally obscuring a manuscript is somewhat abstract and does not clearly distinguish source bias from post-contact historical change.

Prompt 5 would teach the relationship more clearly through a focused public ritual or remembrance scene containing restrained evidence of a preceding raid, rather than depicting an active raid and ceremonial gathering together. Prompt 6 could include a small comparison with dated settlement patterns, weapon evidence, or injuries to show how archaeologists test defensive interpretations. Prompt 7 could more explicitly visualize retelling and change over generations while keeping oral memory and archaeology as complementary, non-identical evidence. Unnecessary title-like suffixes after the em dashes could also be removed to reduce generated text.

userInput.lessonDescription: Recognize warfare as a political and ritual practice that varied by region. Use fortified sites, oral memory, and early accounts carefully to examine raids, revenge, alliances, captive taking, and defense.

steps.text: Before 1500, Brazil contained many distinct peoples and political systems. Conflict could involve a brief raid, a revenge expedition, defense of territory, or a wider alliance—not one shared Indigenous style of warfare.
steps.title: Warfare varied by region

steps.text: War was political because it shaped access to land, routes, resources, and allies. Leaders could gain influence by organizing defense or raids, but that did not always create permanent armies or centralized states.
steps.title: Conflict shaped political power

steps.text: Kinship, marriage, exchange, and shared enemies could connect communities as allies. These ties were flexible: an ally in one conflict might remain neutral or become an opponent in another.
steps.title: Alliances were networks

steps.text: Some conflicts followed cycles of injury and revenge: a death or capture created an obligation to answer. Retaliation could restore honor or social balance, yet it could also produce another grievance and extend the cycle.
steps.title: Revenge could drive raids

steps.text: Captives might be adopted, exchanged, put to work, married into a group, or killed in ritual settings, depending on the people and period. Early accounts describe ritual execution and anthropophagy among some coastal Tupi-speaking groups, but this cannot be generalized to all Indigenous peoples.
steps.title: Captivity had different outcomes

steps.text: Ritual could turn warfare into a public statement about courage, grief, identity, and remembered enemies. That does not make violence merely symbolic: raids caused real deaths, displacement, and fear while also carrying political and spiritual meaning.
steps.title: War could also be ritual

steps.text: Ditches, palisade traces, guarded entrances, and settlements placed for visibility may point to defense. But a fortified site does not reveal the enemy, the exact event, or whether danger was constant, so archaeologists compare dates, weapons, injuries, and settlement patterns.
steps.title: Fortifications are clues, not proof

steps.text: Oral traditions can preserve memories of migrations, enemies, victories, and losses, while changing as communities retell them. They should be read alongside archaeology, not treated as either exact transcripts or invented stories.
steps.title: Oral memory carries history

steps.text: Sixteenth-century Europeans wrote after contact and viewed events through their own religious and political goals. Their reports may describe real practices, but translation problems, exaggeration, epidemics, slavery, and colonial disruption limit what they reveal about life before 1500.
steps.title: Early accounts need caution

steps.text: The strongest interpretation combines independent clues and states uncertainty. A defensive ditch, an oral account of enemies, and an early report may support one another, but they still do not justify treating every region or century as the same.
steps.title: Build claims from several sources

steps.conclusion: Every prompt unnecessarily appends the step title after an em dash, adding text that the image model may render despite the text-restraint requirement. Prompts 0 and 3 are also somewhat broad and abstract: “visible rules” is not concrete visual evidence, and the defense table combines many means of defense rather than focusing on one clear legal-use boundary.

Remove the appended titles and make prompt 0 a tighter procedural before-decision scene with notice, response opportunity, and participation. Prompt 2 could avoid the explanatory “não garante vitória” stamp and instead show serious consideration of arguments alongside an unfavorable outcome. Prompt 3 could use a compact case-file arrangement distinguishing permitted evidence from a clearly excluded illicit item, reducing scene complexity.

userInput.lessonDescription: Relacione devido processo legal, contraditório e ampla defesa à proibição de decisão surpresa. O aluno identifica quando as partes tiveram conhecimento, chance de resposta e possibilidade real de influenciar a decisão.
userInput.lessonTitle: Contraditório, ampla defesa e decisão surpresa

steps.text: A Constituição exige **devido processo legal**: ninguém pode perder liberdade ou bens por um procedimento arbitrário. O processo deve seguir regras justas e dar participação efetiva a quem será afetado.
steps.title: O devido processo é a base

steps.text: O **contraditório** tem três partes: conhecer o que está sendo discutido, ter oportunidade de responder e poder influenciar a decisão. Não basta comunicar a parte se ela não recebe prazo e condições reais para se manifestar.
steps.title: Conhecer, responder e influenciar

steps.text: Influenciar não significa convencer o juiz ou vencer a causa. Significa que os argumentos e provas devem poder ser apresentados antes da decisão e considerados com seriedade na fundamentação.
steps.title: Influência não garante vitória

steps.text: A **ampla defesa** assegura o uso dos meios legais adequados: argumentos, documentos, testemunhas, perícias, recursos e, quando necessário, defesa técnica. “Ampla” não inclui provas ilícitas nem manobras proibidas.
steps.title: Defesa com meios reais

steps.text: O CPC proíbe a **decisão surpresa**: o juiz não pode decidir com base em fundamento sobre o qual as partes não tiveram oportunidade de falar. Isso vale até para questões que o juiz pode reconhecer por iniciativa própria, conforme o art. 10.
steps.title: O juiz também deve ouvir

steps.text: Imagine que autor e réu discutam apenas o pagamento de uma dívida. Se o juiz percebe uma possível prescrição, deve abrir vista às partes antes de encerrar o caso por esse motivo, mesmo podendo analisar a prescrição de ofício.
steps.title: Um fundamento novo

steps.text: Não há surpresa só porque a parte perdeu ou porque o juiz adotou interpretação diferente da que ela queria. O problema aparece quando o fundamento decisivo é novo e não houve conhecimento, tempo de resposta ou possibilidade real de influência.
steps.title: Resultado inesperado não basta

steps.text: Em regra, não se decide contra alguém sem ouvi-lo antes, como prevê o art. 9º do CPC. Há exceções legais, como certas tutelas urgentes; nelas, a medida pode vir primeiro, mas o contraditório ocorre depois, sem ser eliminado.
steps.title: Às vezes, ouvir vem depois

steps.text: Para verificar a garantia, siga três perguntas: a parte conheceu o fundamento e os elementos relevantes? Teve prazo e meios para responder? Sua manifestação poderia ser considerada antes da decisão? Se alguma resposta for não, pode haver violação.
steps.title: Como reconhecer a violação

steps.text: Uma decisão surpresa pode ser anulada quando o vício prejudica a participação da parte. O processo retorna ao ponto necessário para permitir manifestação e nova decisão; a regra protege a construção justa do resultado, não um resultado específico.
steps.title: Consequência da surpresa

Step 1 shows only the resulting file rather than the Windows selection or download/save action. Step 2 introduces “recommended installation options,” which are not necessarily visible when Git Setup first opens. Step 3 shows completed progress but not the key **Install** control or action. Step 8 uses `apt` in a generic Linux terminal, omits the Fedora `dnf` alternative, and could misleadingly imply that `apt` applies to all Linux systems. The appended step-title phrases may also be rendered as unnecessary image text.

Use one unambiguous, tightly cropped state per prompt: show the exact downloads URL for step 0, the Windows download action or resulting `.exe` more explicitly for step 1, the initial Git Setup window without unrelated options for step 2, and the actionable **Install** state for step 3. Identify step 8 specifically as Ubuntu/Debian or incorporate the Fedora alternative without suggesting a mixed interface. userInput.lessonDescription: Download and install Git on your computer, including verification that the installation succeeded

steps.text: Open `https://git-scm.com/downloads` in your web browser. You should see download options for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
steps.title: Open the Git Download Page

steps.text: Click **Windows** and save the `.exe` file. The download may start automatically; when finished, the installer should appear in your Downloads folder.
steps.title: Download Git for Windows

steps.text: Open the downloaded `.exe` file. Approve the security prompt if one appears; the Git Setup window should open.
steps.title: Launch the Windows Installer

steps.text: Keep the recommended settings and click **Next** until **Install** appears. Then click **Install** and wait for the progress bar to finish.
steps.title: Install Git on Windows

steps.text: Click **Finish** when setup completes. If available, leave **Launch Git Bash** selected; a terminal window should open.
steps.title: Finish Windows Setup

steps.text: On macOS, open **Terminal**, type `xcode-select --install`, and press Return. A software installation prompt should appear.
steps.title: Request Git on macOS

steps.text: Click **Install** in the macOS prompt, accept the license, and wait for installation to finish. You should see a completion message.
steps.title: Install Git on macOS

steps.text: On Ubuntu or Debian Linux, open Terminal and run `sudo apt update`. Enter your password if prompted; package information should finish updating without errors.
steps.title: Update Linux Packages

steps.text: Run `sudo apt install git` and type `Y` if prompted. On Fedora, use `sudo dnf install git` instead. Wait until the terminal prompt returns.
steps.title: Install Git on Linux

steps.text: Open a new Terminal or Git Bash window, run `git --version`, and press Enter. Success is confirmed when you see output such as `git version 2.x.x`.
steps.title: Verify the Installation
